sections.report:
I couldn't run the crop and entries scripts because Bash was denied. I worked from the whole image instead. It is about one screen (roughly 1280×800), so it would most likely not have been cut anyway. I did not open the reference entries, and the line about the picture and headline has only an off-list source, so I judged that finding as taste and common sense.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No. The figure (about x 96–656, y 220–420) is a flat diagram: a pale grey block, a dark grey bar and a small blue rounded rectangle on a blue band. The headline and body text are about wider ramps, a covered waiting area, benches facing the water and a kiosk. None of that can be seen in the picture. The caption ("The new north landing, seen from the water at low tide") has to tell the viewer what the shapes are. The one claim the piece makes most of, "ramps now meet the deck at every tide", isn't shown at all, so the picture adds nothing to the article and reads like a placeholder. The blue rounded rectangle (about x 496–606, y 340–364) also looks like the same blue and the same corner radius as the "Sign up" button (x 789–888, y 296–340), so at first it reads as a second button. If this is a stand-in for a photo that hasn't loaded or hasn't been made, it's fine once the real picture is in. If it is the final picture, replace it with a photo or drawing that shows the ramp meeting the deck, which is the thing the reader is told changed. Either way, don't use the interface's action blue inside the picture. Taste and common sense (the source is off-list). Weight: major, because the picture is the largest element on the page and currently says nothing.
2. **Is the copy finished, with no placeholder text and no spelling mistakes?** No. The footer line at about y 749 says "Ferry timetables are a sample for a fixture image. All names and places are invented." This is scaffolding text, not copy for a ferry passenger. On a live page it would make a reader doubt the timetable service the sidebar is selling. Remove it, or swap in the real footer. If this image is only a test fixture, ignore this finding. Common sense. Weight: minor.

**Outside the checklist (copy and the ask).** The form at x 760–1120 asks only for "Your name" and "Home landing". It has no email or phone field. The note under the button says "We send one short note when the timetable changes" but not how it arrives or where to. A first-time viewer can't tell how signing up would ever reach them, and as drawn the sign-up can't work. Add the contact field and say in the note how the message comes: "We email you once when your landing's timetable changes." That also ties "Home landing" to what the reader gets. If the interface critic covers missing form fields, the director may file this there instead. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The piece has one quiet, civic mood that suits a ferry operator's notice. It uses one sans-serif face, a navy and blue palette, plain rectangles, and no decoration. Nothing feels pasted in from somewhere else.
- Both headings say what their sections hold. "Landing stage rebuild" and "Get timetable changes" let a scanning reader know in two seconds what the article is and what the box offers.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; copy finished).

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The headline "Landing stage rebuild" (about x 96–455, y 58–95) is the biggest and heaviest dark text on the page, so the eye starts there with no competition. The sidebar heading "Get timetable changes" (y ~88–115) is also bold but clearly smaller, so it reads as the second stop rather than a rival. The blue Sign up button at about (789, 296) is the strongest patch of colour, which makes it the obvious third stop and the place to act. Keep this order of headline, then form heading, then button.
- The type has a short scale with clear jobs. I count four sizes: the headline, the form heading, body text, and one small size shared by the form labels, the figure caption, the helper note and the footer. The two headings also differ from the text by weight and darker colour, not just size, and the small text is greyer than the body. So each level is distinct by more than one cue, and no two sizes sit close enough to look like a mistake.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space applies. I worked from the whole image, which is about one screen. The crop and entries scripts could not run because Bash was refused, so every position below is judged by eye.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid?** No. The picture runs from x 96 to 656, but the intro text above it runs out to about x 685, and the caption and closing paragraph wrap at their own widths. So the left column has two right edges about 30–40 px apart, and the gap to the card changes from about 75 px beside the text to about 104 px beside the picture. The viewer sees a picture that nearly fills its column but not quite. It looks dropped in at its own size rather than built on the column. Müller-Brockmann (*Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "The photograph in the grid system") says an image takes its width from the columns. Fix: make the picture exactly as wide as the text measure, or set the measure to the picture's width, so the column has one right edge and one gutter to the card. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups formed between unrelated ones?** No. The blue rounded bar in the picture (about x 496–606, y 340–364, presumably the boat) is very close to the "Sign up" button (x 789–887, y 296–339) in colour, corner radius and proportion. Once they have seen the button, a viewer may read the bar as a second control, and both blues compete as accent marks. The page's only call to action loses some of its uniqueness, and the picture may look clickable. The catalog entry is in `references/art-direction.md`, which I could not open, so this rests on common sense. Fix: keep the action blue for controls only, and draw the boat in a colour or shape that does not echo the button. Taste. Weight: minor.
3. **Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion?** No. The left margin is 96 px and the right margin is about 161 px (card edge at x 1119 in a 1280 px frame). The content block is off-centre by about 65 px. That is too much to read as centred and too little to read as a chosen asymmetric layout. It looks like a max-width container that is neither centred nor pinned on purpose. The checklist names no approved source for this line, so it is taste. Fix: either centre the block or commit to a clearly left-weighted layout with a proportioned right margin. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **Clear grouping by space.** Each label sits about 6 px above its field and about 27 px below the previous field. The caption sits close under its picture with a bigger gap before the next paragraph. The headline is closer to its intro than the intro is to the picture. Each group reads as a group without rules.
- **The sidebar is boxed as one group.** The card's top edge (y 57) sits level with the headline's cap height. Its single job (heading, two fields, button, reassurance note) is enclosed in one panel, so the ask stays separate from the article without competing for the left column's reading line.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The footer note at y 749 sits about 220 px below the end of the article. I can't tell whether that space comes from a footer pinned to the viewport bottom or from fixed spacing. Check in a live browser at other heights. Also check how the two columns stack on narrow screens: whether the sign-up card ends up before or after the article.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (one grid with the picture on it; no accidental likenesses; one proportion for the main divisions).

**Section.** Text: applies. The page has a heading, two body paragraphs, a figure caption, a form with labels and helper text, and a footer note.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The body paragraphs are easy to read.** They are set in one plain sans family at about 17 px. The first line of the opening paragraph runs about 66 characters ("The landing stages were rebuilt last spring with wider ramps and a"), which is right at Bringhurst's ideal. The space between lines looks generous enough for that length. The right edge is gently uneven, with no lone word on a last line. Keep this size and this width when revising.
- **Only a few sizes, each with a clear job.** I count about four: the large bold page heading, the smaller bold form heading, body text, and one small grey size. That small size is shared by the caption, the form labels, the helper text and the footer note. Weight and grey do the remaining work instead of extra sizes. The grey small text (cropped at x 760–1160, y 340–460) still looks dark enough and heavy enough to read on white.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The grey small text (caption, labels, helper text, footer note) looks like it passes 4.5:1, but this is by eye only. To confirm, measure its colour against white.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?** No, because of where the accent goes rather than how much of it there is. The page has one saturated hue, the strong blue of the "Sign up" button (about x 789–888, y 296–340). The same blue fills the rounded boat shape in Figure 1 (about x 496–606, y 340–364). That shape is the same colour as the button, has the same rounded corners, and is about the same size, and it is the only saturated thing in the left column. So the eye gets two matching "buttons" and splits between them. The boat looks clickable, and the real action is no longer the one place the accent marks. The rule is that the accent is kept for the main action and interactive state and does not decorate non-interactive content (Apple HIG, Color, accent colors; Material Design 3, Color roles). Fix direction: draw the boat in a colour from the figure's own muted range, such as a darker slate or a desaturated navy, or give it a shape that doesn't read as a control. Keep full-strength blue for "Sign up" alone. Defect (it suggests a click where there is none and dilutes the call to action). Weight: minor. The palette is otherwise calm and the button still reads, but this is the one colour decision that works against the page's job.

**What's working.** The palette stays small and cool: near-black text, gray labels and captions, a pale slate sky and water, and one strong blue. Nothing competes through hue, so the signup button gets its emphasis from saturation alone. The value range is clear: dark headline and body text on white, a mid-gray hull against pale sky and water. Hierarchy and the figure's structure would survive in grayscale.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (strong color kept to a small share: the action blue is reused on the boat in Figure 1)

**Walk (Pictures)**: there is one picture, Figure 1 (x 96–656, y 220–420). The image is about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. The crop script would have printed `no crops`, and Bash is not available here anyway.
- Shows its content, no empty placeholder: **no**. It is four flat blocks: a pale-blue sky, a light-grey box, a dark-grey bar, and a blue rounded bar on a pale-blue band. The caption promises the north landing at low tide, but nothing in it reads as a ramp, deck, benches, kiosk or water level. There is no catalog entry for this line, so it is common sense.
- Full quality: yes. Crop intended: yes. Subject apart from background: yes. One rendering style: yes. Photos: yes (there are none). Line weights: yes (there are no line drawings). One viewpoint: yes (flat side view). Texture: yes (none). No fake depth: yes. Logo and mark lines: yes (no logo).

The one `no` line has no catalog entry, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There is one illustration, Figure 1.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?**
   - **Where:** Figure 1, x 96–656, y 220–420.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the caption says "The new north landing, seen from the water at low tide". What they see is a set of untextured rectangles: a grey box (176–296, 280–330), a dark bar (156–456, 330–360), and a blue rounded bar (496–606, 340–364) on a pale-blue band. It reads as a wireframe placeholder or a half-loaded image, not a picture of a place. The body text makes concrete claims that a picture should prove: wider ramps, a covered waiting area, benches facing the water, a kiosk, and ramps that meet the deck at every tide. The figure shows none of them, so the one visual on the page adds nothing and makes the page look unfinished.
   - **A smaller cost:** the blue rounded bar is the same blue and corner shape as the "Sign up" button (789–888, 296–340). It reads as a stray UI control rather than a boat or a ramp.
   - **Fix:** use a real photo of the north landing, or an illustration detailed enough to show the ramp meeting the deck at low water, since that is the article's main point. If the blocks are an intentional schematic, label the parts (deck, ramp, waiting area, boat) and take the shape out of the interface's button blue. If this is a capture where the real image failed to load, check it in a live browser.
   - **Kind:** defect, judged by common sense (no catalog entry). **Weight:** major.

**What's working.** The figure has a numbered caption in a smaller, quieter grey, placed tight under the image. That ties the picture to its text and keeps it subordinate to the body copy.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether Figure 1 is the final artwork or a fallback shown because the real image failed to load. Check in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content)

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The page has no chart, no table of figures and no dashboard. Figure 1 is a flat drawing of the landing, not data.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

sections.report:
The crop and entries scripts couldn't run because Bash was denied. I judged from the whole 1280×800 image, which is about one screen, and read the Nielsen 5 and 6 entries directly from `references/ux.md`.

**Section.** Interface: applies. There is a sign-up form in the right-hand card at about x 760–1120, y 56–427.

**Findings**
1. **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen, with nothing to remember from another?** The form in the card at y 145–339 asks only for "Your name" and "Home landing", and there is no email or phone field. The note under the button (y 367–388) says "We send one short note when the timetable changes", but you can't tell where it will be sent. So you can't tell what signing up does or how you will hear anything, and if the form really has no contact field, it can't deliver the notes at all. Whatever explains it, such as being signed in, isn't shown. This is common sense more than a catalogued rule: an ask has to say what the user gets and how. Fix: add a labelled contact field, such as "Email", or if the user is already known, show where the notes will go ("Notes go to …"). The fact that the form doesn't say how it reaches you also belongs to this finding. Defect. **Major**.
2. **Do the inputs allow only valid values, by pickers, input types, or disabled options?** (the same problem also fails "nothing to remember", Nielsen 6). The "Home landing" field at about 789–1091, 240–280 is a plain text box drawn exactly like the name field, but landings are a short fixed list. You have to remember and type the operator's exact name for your landing, and "north", "North landing" or a typo may match nothing, so you get no notes or the wrong ones. Nielsen 5 asks for constraints on inputs, and Nielsen 6 for options that are visible rather than recalled. Fix: use a select or picker that lists the landings, and preselect the north landing, since the page is about it. Defect. **Major**.
3. **Are required or optional fields marked?** Neither field at y 145–280 is marked required or optional. You can't tell whether a name is needed just to get timetable notes. Fix: mark the optional field "(optional)", or drop the name field if it isn't needed. Convention. **Minor**.
4. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** Here the problem runs the other way: something that isn't a control looks like one. In the figure, the blue rounded bar at about 496–606, 340–364 has the same saturated blue and corner radius as the Sign up button at 789–888, 296–339. It's meant to be the boat, but it reads as a second button, so the button's colour stops meaning only "press this". Fix: draw the boat with a shape or colour that doesn't match the button style, or keep that blue only for controls. Taste or common sense, since no entry covers decoration that looks pressable. **Minor**.

**What's working.**
- There is exactly one filled button. Sign up is solid blue with white bold text, about 99×43 px, and nothing else on the page competes with it, so the action is clear at a glance.
- The labels sit above their fields and close to them: about 14 px from label to field against about 27 px to the next group, so each label clearly belongs to its own field. The inputs have mid-grey borders that look well above 3:1, so they read as places to type.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the two fields and the button. This is the only way keyboard users can follow the form, so check it in a live browser.
- What happens after Sign up is pressed: whether there is a confirmation and how errors are worded.

**Checklist.** `Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 4 no (every control looks like what it does; inputs allow only valid values; everything needed to act is visible; required or optional fields marked), 1 unsure (focus indicator 2 px at 3:1)`
